questions.title: What is the classic clinical presentation of multiple sclerosis?
questions.question: A young adult presents with a relapsing course of motor weakness and sensory paraesthesia, and MRI shows white-matter lesions consistent with demyelination. Which disease does this describe?

explanations.A: Correct. Multiple sclerosis classically presents with relapsing-remitting attacks of motor weakness and sensory paraesthesia, correlating with demyelinating plaques disseminated in time and space, seen on MRI as characteristic white-matter lesions. Recognising this pattern is central to the clinical/radiological diagnostic criteria for MS, which require lesions disseminated in both time and space.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Guillain-Barre syndrome is an acute, monophasic, ascending peripheral polyneuropathy following infection, not a relapsing CNS demyelinating disease with MRI plaques.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a progressive motor neuron disease with combined upper and lower motor neuron signs, not a relapsing sensory-motor disease with demyelinating plaques.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease is an inherited peripheral neuropathy with a chronic progressive course, not a relapsing CNS disease with plaques on imaging.

questions.learning_objective: State that multiple sclerosis classically presents with relapsing attacks of motor and sensory paraesthesia, correlating with plaques on imaging.

questions.title: Which tumour classically presents as a posterior fossa midline mass in a 5-year-old child?
questions.question: A 5-year-old presents with a midline posterior cranial fossa mass; histology shows sheets of small, primitive round cells. Which tumour is this?

explanations.A: Correct. Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant paediatric brain tumour, classically arising midline in the cerebellum/posterior cranial fossa around age 5, composed histologically of sheets of small, primitive (embryonal) round blue cells. Its tendency to obstruct the fourth ventricle and to metastasise via the CSF ("drop metastases") makes early recognition of this presentation clinically important.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Oligodendroglioma is an adult cerebral hemisphere tumour with a characteristic "fried-egg" clear-halo histology, not a paediatric midline posterior fossa tumour.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Meningioma arises from arachnoid cap cells, typically in adults, and is not composed of sheets of primitive embryonal cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma is a suprasellar (not posterior fossa) tumour arising from Rathke's pouch remnants, with a different histological appearance.

questions.learning_objective: State that medulloblastoma is a childhood embryonal tumour of the posterior cranial fossa, classically midline, composed of sheets of primitive cells.

questions.title: Which pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands?
questions.question: The superior parathyroid glands develop from which pharyngeal pouch?

explanations.A: Correct. The fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands, along with the ultimobranchial body. This counter-intuitive pouch numbering, where the fourth (not third) pouch gives the superior gland, is a classic source of embryology exam confusion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The third pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands (and the thymus), which migrate further caudally, not the superior parathyroids.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The second pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the palatine tonsil, not parathyroid tissue.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The first pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the tympanic cavity and auditory (Eustachian) tube, not parathyroid tissue.

questions.learning_objective: State that the fourth pharyngeal pouch gives rise to the superior parathyroid glands.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, item 15 ("superior parathyroid / Fourth pharyngeal pouch gives")

questions.title: The lateral geniculate body receives its principal input from which structure?
questions.question: The lateral geniculate body of the thalamus receives its principal afferent input from which structure of the visual pathway?

explanations.A: Correct. The optic tract, formed after the partial decussation of fibres at the optic chiasm, carries the contralateral visual field's information and terminates in the lateral geniculate body, its principal input. From there, geniculocalcarine (optic radiation) fibres continue on to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The optic nerve is the pre-chiasmal segment, carrying one eye's entire visual field; it ends at the chiasm, not at the lateral geniculate body.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The optic radiation carries output from the lateral geniculate body onward to the visual cortex, the step after, not the input to it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior colliculus receives some visual input for reflex eye movements, but the lateral geniculate body's principal, conscious-vision input is the optic tract.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lateral geniculate body of the thalamus receives its input from the optic tract.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, item 19 ("optic tract / LGB receives inputs from")

questions.title: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is found within which cistern?
questions.question: As it curves around the splenium of the corpus callosum before draining into the straight sinus, the great cerebral vein (of Galen) lies within which subarachnoid cistern?

explanations.A: Correct. The great cerebral vein of Galen, on its posterior course around the splenium of the corpus callosum toward the straight sinus, lies within the cisterna ambiens (ambient/quadrigeminal cistern region), which wraps around the midbrain. This is a distinct testable fact from the vein's formation by the union of the two internal cerebral veins, which this same lane also covers separately.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cisterna magna lies posterior to the medulla and below the cerebellum, a different CSF space from the great cerebral vein's course.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pontine cistern surrounds the pons, anterior to the brainstem, not the site of the great cerebral vein's course around the splenium.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The chiasmatic cistern surrounds the optic chiasm anteriorly, unrelated to the great cerebral vein's posterior course.

questions.title: Which of these is a commissural fibre tract?
questions.question: Which of the following white matter tracts is classified as a commissural fibre, connecting the two cerebral hemispheres?

explanations.A: Correct. Forceps major is formed by splenial fibres of the corpus callosum sweeping into each occipital lobe, connecting the two occipital lobes across the midline, making it a commissural fibre tract. It is the corpus callosum's largest single commissure alongside forceps minor, which instead connects the two frontal lobes via the genu.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The cuneocerebellar tract is a projection tract carrying proprioceptive input to the cerebellum, not a commissural tract connecting the two hemispheres.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The internal capsule is a projection fibre pathway connecting the cortex to lower centres (e.g. corticospinal fibres), not a commissural tract.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior longitudinal fasciculus is an association fibre tract connecting areas within the same hemisphere, not a commissural tract.

questions.learning_objective: State that forceps major is a commissural fibre of the corpus callosum connecting the two occipital lobes.

questions.title: Isoflurane is used with caution in which patient group because of coronary steal?
questions.question: Isoflurane's coronary vasodilating effect makes it risky in patients with which condition, due to coronary steal?

explanations.A: Correct. Isoflurane's coronary vasodilation can produce coronary steal in patients with ischaemic heart disease: blood is diverted from stenotic, poorly-autoregulating vessels toward normal vessels that dilate more readily, worsening perfusion to already-ischaemic myocardium. Anaesthetists therefore favour agents with a more neutral coronary vascular profile in patients with significant coronary artery disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Coronary steal is a coronary artery disease phenomenon; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is not the condition specifically linked to isoflurane's coronary steal risk.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chronic kidney disease is not the condition specifically associated with isoflurane's coronary steal risk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Well-controlled hypertension without coronary artery stenosis does not carry the same coronary steal risk as established ischaemic heart disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that isoflurane is used with caution in ischaemic heart disease because of coronary steal.

questions.title: Long-term haloperidol therapy causes which movement disorder?
questions.question: A patient on long-term haloperidol develops involuntary lip smacking and tongue protrusion. Which condition is this?

explanations.A: Correct. Long-term (chronic) haloperidol therapy causes tardive dyskinesia, involuntary repetitive orofacial movements (lip smacking, tongue protrusion, chewing), attributed to dopamine receptor supersensitivity after prolonged blockade, and often irreversible even after stopping the drug. This late complication is often irreversible even after stopping the drug, distinguishing it from haloperidol's earlier, reversible extrapyramidal effects.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute dystonia is an early (hours to days), reversible extrapyramidal effect of antipsychotics, not the late orofacial movement disorder from long-term use.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Akathisia is a subjective restlessness occurring early in antipsychotic treatment, not the late orofacial dyskinesia of chronic use.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Drug-induced parkinsonism (rigidity, bradykinesia) occurs early to mid-treatment and is reversible, distinct from the late, often-irreversible orofacial movements of tardive dyskinesia.

questions.learning_objective: State that long-term haloperidol therapy causes tardive dyskinesia, presenting with orofacial involuntary movements.

questions.title: Which drug is given as a monthly IV infusion when first-line MS therapy fails?
questions.question: A patient with multiple sclerosis fails first-line disease-modifying therapy. Which monoclonal antibody, given as a monthly intravenous infusion, is used next?

explanations.A: Correct. Natalizumab, a monoclonal antibody against alpha-4 integrin that blocks leukocyte migration across the blood-brain barrier, is a second-line, highly-effective disease-modifying therapy for multiple sclerosis, used when first-line agents fail and given as a monthly IV infusion. Its use is limited by the risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a serious JC virus-related brain infection that requires monitoring.
explanations.B: Incorrect. High-dose IV methylprednisolone is used for acute MS relapses/attacks, not as ongoing disease-modifying therapy after first-line failure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interferon beta is itself a first-line disease-modifying agent, not the second-line option used after first-line failure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Varenicline is a smoking-cessation drug, unrelated to multiple sclerosis treatment.

questions.learning_objective: State that natalizumab is used for multiple sclerosis, given as a monthly intravenous infusion, when first-line therapy fails.

questions.title: Which antiepileptic is safest for a child with absence epilepsy?
questions.question: Which antiepileptic drug is considered safest for a child with uncomplicated absence epilepsy, with the least effect on cognition and learning?

explanations.A: Correct. Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, the mechanism underlying absence seizures, and is regarded as the safest option for uncomplicated childhood absence epilepsy, with a more favourable cognitive/learning profile than the alternatives. This favourable safety profile makes it the preferred choice when sparing a child's cognition and learning during long-term antiepileptic therapy is a priority.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Valproate also covers absence seizures but carries a broader systemic and, in females, teratogenic/reproductive safety burden, making it a less favoured first choice when sparing cognition is the priority.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phenytoin is not effective for, and can worsen, absence seizures, and is not the safest choice here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Carbamazepine can worsen absence seizures and is not indicated for this seizure type.

questions.learning_objective: State that ethosuximide is the safest antiepileptic for absence epilepsy in a child, with the least effect on cognition and learning.

questions.title: Growth hormone secretion decreases during which sleep stage?
questions.question: Growth hormone secretion, which peaks during slow-wave (deep) sleep, decreases during which other sleep stage?

explanations.A: Correct. Growth hormone's largest, most reliable secretory pulse occurs during slow-wave (deep, N3) sleep; correspondingly, its secretion decreases during REM sleep, when many neuroendocrine and autonomic patterns shift away from the deep non-REM state. This sleep-stage-linked secretion pattern is one reason adequate slow-wave sleep is considered important for growth hormone-dependent processes such as childhood growth.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Stage N1 is light sleep at sleep onset, not the stage specifically associated with decreased growth hormone secretion relative to slow-wave sleep.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Stage N2 is an intermediate non-REM stage; growth hormone's characteristic decrease is specifically described relative to REM sleep, not N2.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sleep onset itself is not the stage of decreased growth hormone secretion; the described decrease is specific to REM sleep.

questions.learning_objective: State that growth hormone secretion decreases during REM sleep and peaks during slow-wave (deep) sleep.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, item 32 ("growth hormone / Dec in REM sleep")

questions.title: Which hypothalamic region functions as the heat-loss centre for thermoregulation?
questions.question: Which region of the hypothalamus functions as the heat-loss (cooling) centre for thermoregulation?

explanations.A: Correct. The anterior hypothalamus (anterior/preoptic area) functions as the heat-loss centre, triggering cooling responses (cutaneous vasodilation, sweating) when core temperature rises; direct injury to this region can raise temperature through heat-loss failure rather than true infective fever. Because the anterior hypothalamus is not itself an infection sensor, direct injury to it can raise temperature through heat-loss failure rather than a true infective fever.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior hypothalamus functions as the heat-conservation/heat-generation centre, the opposite role to the anterior hypothalamus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral hypothalamus is chiefly associated with the hunger/feeding centre, not thermoregulatory heat loss.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The paraventricular nucleus is chiefly associated with oxytocin/vasopressin synthesis and autonomic/neuroendocrine output, not the primary heat-loss centre.

questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior hypothalamus functions as the heat-loss centre for thermoregulation.

questions.title: Which EEG wave characterises deep (slow-wave) sleep?
questions.question: Which EEG wave frequency band, the lowest-frequency and highest-amplitude of the standard rhythms, characterises deep slow-wave (stage N3) sleep?

explanations.A: Correct. Delta waves are the lowest-frequency (under 4 Hz), highest-amplitude EEG rhythm, and they characterise deep, slow-wave sleep (stage N3), the stage with the highest arousal threshold. This contrasts with the fast, desynchronised, wake-like EEG pattern of REM sleep, which paradoxically resembles wakefulness despite being a deep sleep stage behaviourally.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alpha waves are seen in relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed, not deep sleep.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Beta waves are the fastest, lowest-amplitude rhythm, seen in alert wakefulness and REM sleep, not deep slow-wave sleep.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Theta waves are seen in light (stage N1) sleep and drowsiness, an intermediate frequency band, not the signature of deep slow-wave sleep.

questions.learning_objective: State that delta waves on the EEG characterise deep (slow-wave) sleep.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, item 35 ("DElta wave / Deep sleep")

questions.title: Consciously recalling a specific past personal event is an example of which memory type?
questions.question: A teenager consciously recalls the details of her own tenth birthday party. Which type of memory does this exemplify?

explanations.A: Correct. Consciously recalling a specific personal event tied to a particular time and place is a classic example of episodic explicit (declarative) memory, which requires deliberate conscious retrieval and depends on the medial temporal lobe/hippocampal system. This episodic explicit memory depends anatomically on the medial temporal lobe/hippocampal system, distinguishing it from implicit, performance-based memory.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Implicit (procedural) memory is expressed through performance of skills or habits without conscious recall, not through consciously remembering a specific past event.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Semantic memory is explicit but stores general facts and knowledge, not a memory tied to a specific personal experience.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Working memory is the brief, active holding of information for immediate use, not the long-term recall of a past personal event.

questions.learning_objective: State that explicit (declarative) memory is exemplified by the conscious recall of a personal event.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, item 36 ("teenager remembers her 10th birthday / Explicit memory conscious recall example")

questions.title: Consolidation of memory is chiefly a function of which brain system?
questions.question: The process of consolidating a newly formed short-term memory into a stable long-term memory chiefly depends on which brain system?

explanations.A: Correct. Memory consolidation depends on the limbic system, chiefly the hippocampus and adjacent medial temporal lobe structures together with the Papez circuit, which bind distributed cortical representations of an experience into a lasting memory over time. Damage to these limbic structures, as in bilateral hippocampal lesions, characteristically impairs consolidation of new memories while often sparing older, already-consolidated ones.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The basal ganglia are chiefly involved in movement/procedural learning circuits, not the consolidation of declarative memory.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cerebellum is chiefly involved in motor coordination and some forms of procedural/implicit learning, not declarative memory consolidation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The reticular activating system governs arousal and consciousness level, not the specific process of memory consolidation.

questions.learning_objective: State that consolidation of memory is a function of the limbic system.

field_notes.asu: EOM - paper 2 cns 2019.pdf, item 38 ("consolidation of memory / Function of Limbic System")
